title: Robotics Systems Survey
summary: The reviewed workflows support a local layer linking setup, execution and recording evidence.
Agent consumption is a first-class design constraint: structured summaries, explicit uncertainty, stable IDs and access to underlying evidence.
Lab-to-startup adoption is a distribution hypothesis. Validate repeat use across researchers and a second project before treating it as a growth channel.

method.selection: Primary focus: onboard and robot-side Linux compute for physical experiments, including local inference, resource policies, IPC, lifecycle and recording. Remote inference is tracked as an operational dependency. Simulation studies provide secondary workflow comparisons.
method.coverage: 7 paper case studies; 5 project implementations plus 2 dependency repositories inspected at pinned commits. HALTER release is README-only; AllDayNav implementation is unverified. Static analysis only. University robot inventories and team rosters, plus conference workshop rationale/program, supplement the project evidence. Linked presentations are tracked separately from inspected material. Expanded pass adds 21 physical project/platform dossiers from papers, university sites and setup documentation; two include selected implementation files. Review depth varies per dossier.
method.smallTeams: Paper author counts describe publications. KIT provides a dated lab roster; current staffing and purchasing authority remain open questions elsewhere.
method.time: Base paper snapshots are v1; RoboCerebra v2 was additionally inspected. Repository snapshots were collected 25 October 2026 and can postdate publication experiments.
method.gaps: Public code establishes mechanisms and some failure paths. It does not establish incident frequency, budgets or purchase intent; those need partner trials and customer evidence.
method.decision: The strongest product hypothesis is a local session/evidence layer that integrates existing launchers and writers. The survey supplies concrete integration targets.

profiles.name: AutoEval
profiles.headline: A robot evaluation station that runs through the night
profiles.hardware: WidowX 250 · Logitech C920

facts.label: Experiment
facts.value: Policy rollouts → score → reset → verify → next trial. Five demonstrated tasks.

facts.label: Observed constraint
facts.value: Three human interventions in a 24-hour run. Scores drifted after about eight hours, attributed to motor heating; authors introduced 20-minute cooling pauses every six hours.

facts.label: Compute
facts.value: Policy serving is separable from the robot action server. Exact GPU model for the inspected deployment remains unverified.

facts.label: Evaluation-host recording
facts.value: Episode frames, actions and proprioception are buffered in the evaluation process, then saved as metadata JSON and trajectory pickle. The host’s physical placement is unverified.

facts.label: Recovery already present
facts.value: Motor checks/reboots, reset retries and operator confirmation. Motor-failed rollouts can be repeated; retry counts and failure flags are logged.

facts.label: Vendor host baseline
facts.value: WidowX X-Series supports external Ubuntu hosts; vendor instructions cover AMD64 and Raspberry Pi 4B ARM64.

facts.label: External reporting / export
facts.value: Hugging Face is an upload destination in the logger; W&B provides reporting. Upload runs synchronously after local save. These integrations provide no evidence that the evaluation process runs onboard.

facts.label: Inferred · Robot-server hardware
facts.value: 1 · Intel NUC-class x86 mini-PC — medium confidence, explicitly suggested by the project README. 2 · General x86 Linux workstation — lower confidence; it supports the same robot-server role. Confirm via: Host model / CPU inventory.

facts.label: Inferred · Robot-server Linux
facts.value: 1 · Ubuntu 20.04 + ROS 1 Noetic — medium confidence: ROS 1 launch path and vendor-supported Ubuntu host. 2 · Ubuntu 18.04 + ROS 1 Melodic — lower confidence, a compatible older ROS 1 generation. Exact image is unreported. Confirm via: OS release and ROS_DISTRO from the robot server.

profiles.seam: Make every evaluation attempt traceable across the robot server, policy server, resets, cooling periods and recording completion.
profiles.evidence: The inspected loop collects frames/actions/proprioception in memory and calls log_episode after the rollout. It replaces eval_infos when retrying a motor-failed rollout. The saved metadata supplies a fixed robot_name="widowx_drawer" even though multiple robot IDs are supported.
profiles.offer: Wrap one existing evaluation command. Produce an attempt ledger linking checkpoint identity, actual machine configuration, cooling/reset/intervention events and flushed recording segments. Preserve their W&B reports.
profiles.test: Use a controlled interrupted recording and a policy-server restart in a safe test setup. Every started attempt should remain accounted for, with explicit incomplete/invalid status and links to its surviving evidence.
profiles.limits: Static source review. Current robot_eval_logger auto_eval branch and agentlace dependencies were also inspected; their deployed revisions are unverified. Live behavior and performance were not measured.
profiles.adoption: Strong discovery lead: owns exactly the sustained-evaluation workflow. Purchasing authority and willingness to add a runtime remain unknown.

profiles.name: AnywhereVLA
profiles.headline: A complete mobile manipulation stack on Orin and x86
profiles.hardware: Onboard Jetson Orin NX 16 GB + Intel NUC Core i7 / 32 GB RAM
profiles.horizon: Multi-stage missions; reported tasks under 2.5 minutes

facts.label: Compute split
facts.value: Orin handles semantic perception and manipulation; NUC handles SLAM, exploration and control. Sensors include RealSense and Velodyne.

facts.label: Experiment
facts.value: Explore → locate → approach → manipulate in a multi-room lab. Paper reports 46% overall success, with manipulation and exploration failure modes.

facts.label: Recorded example
facts.value: README describes a 96.2-second, 1 GiB ROS 2 bag with LiDAR, IMU, RGB and camera calibration. This example establishes recording use; campaign-scale integrity is unverified.

facts.label: Launch already present
facts.value: A shell entry point selects CPU/GPU/hardware groups; Compose bundles ROS services. The GPU configuration binds host driver libraries, devices, model and configuration directories.

profiles.seam: Capture the effective state of two machines and the complete mission, including process startup, configuration mounts, calibration and topic continuity.
profiles.evidence: The pinned launcher checks paths such as "docker compose.yaml" while checked-in files are named "docker-compose.yaml". Some sequential Compose calls use foreground mode; Python bridges are backgrounded without a cleanup trap in this file. The SmolVLA configuration depends on host Tegra/TensorRT paths and local mounts.
profiles.offer: A preflight and session wrapper around their current Compose stack: resolve all paths, verify required nodes/topics, snapshot actual host/container/model state and emit a mission timeline alongside their bag.
profiles.test: Reproduce the documented launch on their supported image; report missing services before a mission begins. Then intentionally interrupt a non-actuating service and verify detection, recording annotation and cleanup.
profiles.limits: Launcher mismatches were found by static inspection; deployment was not reproduced. Authors may use private or component-specific launch paths. Task reasoning and grasp failures require their domain work.
profiles.adoption: Closest hardware match in this sample. Offer to solve a specific reproducibility problem; verify whether the public setup represents their active workflow.

profiles.name: HALTER
profiles.headline: Automating the scoring and reset between long tasks
profiles.hardware: Franka Panda · Robotiq 2F-85 · 3 RGB-D cameras

facts.label: Experiment
facts.value: Scene graph keyframes drive rollout scoring, reset planning, execution and verification. Twelve reset skills use 30–50 demonstrations each.

facts.label: Observed tradeoff
facts.value: Across 100 episodes, operator time falls from 88 to 24 minutes; mean cycle time increases from 53 to 121 seconds versus manual operation.

facts.label: Reliability
facts.value: 76% reset success and 91% verification accuracy in the reported experiment. Human escalation still matters.

facts.label: Implementation visibility
facts.value: The inspected main tree contains only README.md; it says the code release is in progress. Logging, checkpointing and launch behavior cannot yet be inspected.

facts.label: University lab context
facts.value: KIT IRL roster: 8 PhD researchers and 7 research assistants, plus group head and secretariat; page updated April 2026. RSS 2025 lists Lioutikov presenting a force-aware manipulation tasksuite.

facts.label: Vendor control baseline
facts.value: Franka FCI / libfranka C++; PREEMPT_RT Linux and gigabit Ethernet recommended. HALTER deployment versions remain unresolved.

facts.label: Inferred · Control host
facts.value: 1 · External x86 Ubuntu workstation with libfranka / FCI and PREEMPT_RT — medium confidence as a Panda control baseline. 2 · Separate real-time control PC plus perception/planning host — lower confidence; this separates control from foundation-model work. Confirm via: Process-to-host diagram and robot control library.

facts.label: Inferred · Linux generation
facts.value: 1 · Ubuntu 22.04 with a compatible real-time kernel — low confidence. 2 · Ubuntu 20.04 with a compatible real-time kernel — low confidence. Both are vendor-supported; paper evidence does not rank the installed version. Confirm via: OS release, kernel version and libfranka version.

profiles.seam: Make reset/scoring decisions and interventions inspectable across the complete evaluation cycle.
profiles.evidence: The paper measures both operator effort and cycle time. A useful runtime must preserve that distinction and account for verification errors and reset attempts.
profiles.offer: Propose an event schema for rollout → score → reset plan → skill execution → verification → intervention, with evidence links for every decision and machine-readable summaries.
profiles.test: Once code is available, reconstruct one failed reset from saved events and images. Measure operator attention, valid trials per hour and false acceptance separately.
profiles.limits: Paper-level evidence; code inspection is blocked by release status. Runtime tooling would support their scoring/reset method. GPU model and ROS usage remain unverified.
profiles.adoption: Useful workflow interview now; integration discussion depends on code availability and the team’s current priorities.

profiles.name: RoboCerebra
profiles.headline: Long-horizon evaluation with disturbances and partial progress
profiles.hardware: Simulated Panda · paper uses 8 × A100

facts.label: Experiment
facts.value: 100 task variants; long sequences test planning and memory. Disturbance and task-progress evaluation are central.

facts.label: Environment
facts.value: Evaluation loads BDDL task descriptions, HDF5 demonstration states and goal metadata; Panda environment uses a 20 Hz control frequency and offscreen cameras.

facts.label: Tracking already present
facts.value: Run IDs, checkpoint paths, seeds, configuration, task results and partial-success metrics saved to JSON; text logs, rollout videos and optional W&B.

facts.label: Resume semantics
facts.value: The resume helper updates subtask completion state for earlier goal steps. This supports the evaluation protocol; crash recovery and durable replay of a whole worker require separate investigation.

profiles.seam: Preserve exact benchmark inputs and the distinction between genuine policy progress, restored state and protocol-induced completion.
profiles.evidence: JSON records checkpoint and configuration paths plus several evaluation flags. The inspected save function writes the results file directly. Task loading can skip absent files and returns structured errors; resume mutates progress accounting.
profiles.offer: Add content hashes for checkpoint/task/state inputs, an append-only episode ledger and a comparison report that exposes changed protocols, exclusions and synthetic completion events.
profiles.test: Run a tiny repeated suite with fixed inputs; interrupt it between episodes. Reconcile every scheduled case, preserve completed evidence and flag protocol changes before producing A/B summaries.
profiles.limits: The paper’s 8-A100 setup does not establish the minimum hardware needed for this harness. Current repository code can differ from the publication snapshot. Whole-process crash recovery was not demonstrated.
profiles.adoption: Accessible maintainer and inspectable evaluation code. A narrow contribution could test adoption quickly; the commercial path would need evidence from wider reuse.

profiles.name: RoboCasa365
profiles.headline: Benchmark scale makes protocol identity consequential
profiles.hardware: MuJoCo CPU physics + GPU rendering · GH200 training example

facts.label: Experiment
facts.value: Simulation benchmark with 600+ human demonstration hours and 1,600+ synthetic hours. Runs at 20 Hz; asynchronous environments can scale across CPU/GPU resources.

facts.label: Protocol changed
facts.value: v1.0.1 announcement on 12 May 2026 increases task horizons by 1.5× and asks evaluators to update.

facts.label: Tracking primitives
facts.value: The inspected environment helper accepts seed, camera, object split and layout/style configuration; a simple rollout utility saves video. Dataset registries define task assets and horizon metadata.

facts.label: Semantic evidence
facts.value: October 2026 release adds per-frame subtask labels across 300 composite tasks, supporting more precise analysis of where execution diverges.

facts.label: University lab context
facts.value: RPL publishes a multi-embodiment robot inventory, including four Pandas and shared HCRL platforms. Compute allocation and use for this project remain project-specific questions.

facts.label: State-rich demonstrations
facts.value: Collector preserves HDF5 states/actions, model XML, episode metadata and RoboCasa/robosuite/MuJoCo versions.

profiles.seam: Bind every result to the exact task definition, asset versions and horizon policy, then expose compatibility before comparisons.
profiles.evidence: A documented 1.5× horizon update changes the time available to succeed. A checkpoint name and aggregate success rate cannot alone establish an equivalent evaluation protocol.
profiles.offer: An evaluation manifest and compatibility checker for a small RoboCasa sweep, with per-subtask evidence links using the existing annotations.
profiles.test: Compare manifests before and after a deliberate horizon or dataset change; the report should name the difference and separate compatible subsets.
profiles.limits: Selected helpers and registry inspected; external training/evaluation integrations may already provide additional provenance. Large established ecosystem; prospective partnership needs validation.
profiles.adoption: Useful distribution/integration conversation if a working adapter earns repeat use. Public author page is verified; email was not established in this pass.

profiles.name: NAVSIM v2
profiles.people: Multi-institution author team; small-team status unverified
profiles.headline: AV evaluation needs an auditable scenario denominator
profiles.hardware: Recorded driving scenes + learned agent inference
profiles.horizon: Short scenario evaluations combined in two stages

facts.label: Experiment
facts.value: Pseudo-simulation extends recorded scenes with off-trajectory views and two-stage evaluation. This is an AV benchmark workflow, with a horizon distinct from overnight robot operation.

facts.label: Configuration already present
facts.value: Hydra stores expanded configuration under the output directory. Worker configuration controls parallel execution.

facts.label: Recording already present
facts.value: Per-scenario validity, token and scores are collected; timestamped CSV and failed-token summaries are emitted.

facts.label: Coverage behavior
facts.value: The runner intersects scene tokens with metric-cache tokens. Missing caches generate warnings and those scenarios are skipped.

profiles.seam: Make expected, attempted, excluded and successfully scored scenario counts explicit in every result and A/B comparison.
profiles.evidence: The inspected runner reports missing cache tokens, handles scenario exceptions and produces validity fields. An experiment runtime could carry this information into a durable, comparable experiment manifest with cache and software identities.
profiles.offer: A preflight coverage check and result adapter that preserves NAVSIM metrics while linking configuration, checkpoint, cache identity and every scheduled scenario outcome.
profiles.test: Remove one test cache entry in an isolated fixture; require the report to show the exact excluded token and the denominator change. Compare common-token results explicitly.
profiles.limits: Static inspection establishes the skip behavior; it does not establish that published results are invalid. The inspected runner is current HEAD, which may include changes since the 2025 paper. Deployment GPU details vary by agent.
profiles.adoption: Strong technical comparator. Larger existing infrastructure and established maintainers raise the bar for useful incremental value.

profiles.name: AllDayNav
profiles.headline: A robot and remote learning server evolve together
profiles.hardware: Go2 · vendor 8-core configurations; optional Orin expansion · paper uses remote H100

facts.label: Compute
facts.value: Paper reports 40 H100s for pretraining, 8 for online learning and approximately 5 Hz inference on one H100 during deployment.

facts.label: Experiment
facts.value: Five simulated scenes and three physical environments. Sensor data goes to a remote server; a web bridge returns controls and logs trajectories.

facts.label: Evaluation protocol
facts.value: Held-out instructions and fixed starting positions; evaluations occur at wall-clock checkpoints. Memory and policy evolve across episodes.

facts.label: Implementation visibility
facts.value: No official implementation link was found on the project page or in the targeted repository search. Detailed logging and recovery claims remain unverified.

facts.label: Vendor platform stack
facts.value: SDK2 / Cyclone DDS; ROS 2 Foxy or Humble host support. Optional Orin expansion. Paper-specific edition and installed software need confirmation.

facts.label: Inferred · Go2 edition
facts.value: 1 · EDU / research configuration — medium confidence. Sensor access and autonomous command integration fit the vendor development offering. 2 · Pro with a custom bridge — lower confidence; the paper’s web-control path could support a custom integration. Confirm via: Ask for edition or SDK connection method.

facts.label: Inferred · Robot-side inference hardware
facts.value: 1 · Built-in controller plus lightweight sensor/control bridge — medium confidence: the paper places VLA inference on a remote H100. 2 · Orin expansion handles local sensing/bridge work — lower confidence: vendor offers it, with no installation evidence in the paper. Confirm via: Robot equipment photo or device inventory.

facts.label: Inferred · Linux / middleware host
facts.value: 1 · Ubuntu 22.04 + ROS 2 Humble / Cyclone DDS — low confidence, based on the recommended vendor development stack. 2 · Ubuntu 20.04 + Foxy / Cyclone DDS — low confidence, also vendor-tested. These describe a possible bridge/development host; robot firmware OS is unresolved. Confirm via: Bridge host OS release and package manifest.

profiles.seam: Tie each physical episode to the policy and memory state actually used across the network boundary.
profiles.evidence: The described architecture spans robot sensing, remote inference, a control bridge and online updates. The paper documents the learning protocol; deployment provenance and restart behavior need a maintainer discussion.
profiles.offer: A proposed cross-machine session manifest: sensor timestamps, server/model identity, memory snapshot lineage, action age and network interruption events.
profiles.test: Start with one recorded episode and reconstruct its model/memory/transport lineage. Later validate explicit stale-action handling in a safe isolated setup with the team.
profiles.limits: Paper-only architecture review. “Lifelong” does not establish an uninterrupted 24-hour deployment. This resource profile should not be generalized to a small independent lab.
profiles.adoption: Useful boundary case for hybrid architecture; weaker evidence for a lightweight on-device initial customer.

findings.title: An interrupted episode can lose its evidence
findings.evidence: Mobile ALOHA holds an episode in RAM before HDF5; ToddlerBot saves in finally; OpenTeach depth/state arrays write after interruption. DROID queues incremental HDF5 writes and drains them on close.
findings.meaning: Persistence behavior varies within the same research workflow. File format alone does not describe what survives process failure.
findings.build: Record completion, buffered bytes, last persisted sample and termination reason. Test interruption and disk-full behavior per writer.

findings.title: Hardware configuration belongs in the run record
findings.evidence: The sample spans Orin hosts, Intel control PCs, remote inference servers and MCU sensor bridges. FAST-LIVO2 specifies a 32GB NUC; AnywhereVLA splits work across Orin and NUC; VibeCheck has separate sensor MCUs and a ROS2 host.
findings.meaning: A useful comparison identifies which process ran on which machine and the settings actually active during the run.
findings.build: Snapshot device, kernel, driver, memory, power mode, affinity and process placement at session start; report changes.

findings.title: Readiness already has domain-specific meaning
findings.evidence: MRS checks odometry, hardware freshness, arming and offboard mode; Mobile ALOHA waits for both grippers; Walk These Ways uses operator calibration gates.
findings.meaning: Starting processes is only one stage. Preserve existing readiness checks and their results as part of the attempt.
findings.build: Adapters for setup → ready → active → stop → finalize, with timestamps, ownership and failure reasons.

findings.title: Capture formats are plural—even within one run
findings.evidence: OpenTeach combines AVI, HDF5 and metadata; UMI combines a replay buffer, MP4 and a Zarr dataset; BeyondMimic configures MCAP. ACFR adds file splitting and compression controls.
findings.meaning: Adoption requires linking existing artifacts. A common session identity can span their different formats and storage paths.
findings.build: An artifact index with schemas, time ranges, checksums, source process and finalization state; adapters for existing recorders.

findings.title: Existing resource controls are an integration surface
findings.evidence: TidyBot sets real-time kernel/governor policy; Cheetah configures scheduler/memory locking; iiwa_setup pins logical CPUs; Upkie uses real-time scheduling.
findings.meaning: The survey supports observing and checking effective policy. It does not measure how often contention causes failed experiments.
findings.build: Explain requested versus effective settings, then attach latency and sensor-age evidence to the run.

findings.title: Replay has several meanings
findings.evidence: DROID has physical action playback with calibration warnings; MUSE documents rosbag clock replay; UMI stores training episodes; AutoEval stores per-episode trajectories and metadata.
findings.meaning: An artifact’s existence leaves questions about restartability, physical reset state and comparison validity.
findings.build: Declare replay mode and prerequisites; compare model/configuration, calibration, initial state, intervention and excluded-attempt history.

proposals.name: A run manifest around an existing command
proposals.scope: Wrap one real workflow’s existing launcher and recorder. Link each participating machine and process to one attempt ID.
proposals.deliverable: Resolved machine/config snapshot; stage events; process exits; artifact paths and completion state.
proposals.agent: Versioned JSON schema, stable IDs, query-by-run and bounded time-window reads; source references on every diagnosis.
proposals.validation: A researcher uses the bundle to explain an interrupted or incomparable run, then keeps it enabled for the next experiment.
proposals.risk: Multi-host clocks, credentials and missing recorder callbacks. Start with one supported setup and expose remaining gaps.

proposals.name: Recording health and finalization
proposals.scope: Integrate existing MCAP, HDF5 and Python recorders. Start with formats and failure paths a partner actually uses.
proposals.deliverable: Buffer/disk telemetry; last persisted sample; drop counters where observable; explicit incomplete artifacts after interruption.
proposals.agent: Structured coverage report with gaps, affected streams, time ranges and links to raw evidence.
proposals.validation: Injected process kills and disk-full cases produce accurate incomplete-run reports; a partner uses those reports during real data collection.
proposals.risk: Durability depends on the writer, filesystem and storage hardware. Verify each supported combination before making guarantees.

proposals.name: Configuration-aware A/B diagnosis
proposals.scope: Compare two attempts and their effective environment, then inspect timing or artifact differences with existing tools.
proposals.deliverable: Machine/policy/configuration diff; latency and sensor-age summaries; replay prerequisites; attempt exclusions.
proposals.agent: Typed comparisons, confidence and provenance; drill down from summary to samples without parsing dashboards.
proposals.validation: A team uses a comparison to reproduce or explain a regression and asks to apply it to another workflow.
proposals.risk: Configuration differences establish hypotheses. Causal claims require controlled reruns; safety-related changes require the team’s approval.

hardware.value: Onboard: Jetson Orin NX 16 GB plus Intel NUC Core i7 with 32 GB RAM.
Orin NX 16GB: 8× Cortex-A78AE. Separate NUC Core i7; exact CPU model unreported.
Orin: Ampere, 1,024 CUDA cores, 32 Tensor cores; compute capability 8.7 (sm_87).
Orin: 16GB shared LPDDR5, 128-bit, rated 102.4GB/s. NUC: 32GB system RAM.
Onboard perception/inference on Orin; SLAM, Nav2 and exploration on NUC. Effective power mode, clocks, thermal limits and storage device need verification.

runtime.value: GPU side: perception and SmolVLA; CPU side: SLAM, maps, Nav2 and exploration. The split allocates work across machines; the paper does not give per-process budgets.

Checked-in image uses l4t-pytorch:r36.4.0 and JetPack 6.1 apt repositories with ROS 2 Humble. x86 Compose variant specifies CUDA 12.4.1, PyTorch 2.6.0 and Ubuntu 22.04. These are build configurations.
Compose requests GPU visibility and host networking; no CPU/memory quota or explicit GPU execution priority is configured.
ROS 2 image/state/control topics use depth-10 queues; Fast DDS XML selects the middleware transport. The node stores latest images and publishes target-state arrays.

SmolVLA config: FP16, device=auto, requested 20 Hz timer. Inference runs synchronously inside the timer callback; image callbacks retain the latest array without its header timestamp. No stale-image rejection appears in this wrapper.

lifecycle.value: Compose starts interactive containers; ROS entrypoints source Humble then launch nodes. Model inference runs on a configured timer; no watchdog is shown.

Hardware Compose has restart directives commented out. The top-level shell script backgrounds two bridge processes and has no cleanup trap; launch filenames also diverge from checked-in Compose paths.
Commands toggle SmolVLA active/inactive; repeated commands toggle again. Inference exceptions log warnings and leave the timer active.
No explicit taskset/cpuset/chrt, nvpmodel/jetson_clocks, CUDA stream priority or MPS configuration found in the inspected first-party launch/configuration files. Live machine settings remain unknown.
Requested/effective host settings and stale-sensor rejection are not recorded by the inspected wrapper.

recording.value: LeRobot recording uses three RealSense streams at 640×360, 15 fps; episode task and robot/camera IDs are configured in CLI.
LeRobot writer is configured for 8 image threads per camera and 2 writer processes; recording runs 25×60s episodes with 2s resets.
Leader script enables resume; video=false. Evaluation example uses video=true with 5×20s episodes and 10s resets. Crash recovery unverified.
Dataset repo/task, robot IDs and RealSense serials label the run; leader script sets resume=true and record-data script points to dataset repo/path.
Inspected the listed first-party source for the described system; no additional recording format is documented in that scope.

hardware.value: Robot server: Intel NUC suggested. Evaluation process and optional remote policy server run separately.
Intel NUC suggested; installed CPU model and core count unreported.
CUDA policy inference supported; GPU model unreported.
Host RAM and GPU VRAM unreported.
WidowX vendor supports external Ubuntu hosts and documents AMD64 and Raspberry Pi 4B ARM64 setup. AutoEval suggests NUC; exact deployed host remains unresolved.

Vendor baselines, optional expansions and publication-confirmed configurations retain separate labels; current documentation can postdate the experiment. Baseline means robot-side or explicitly identified local-host functionality. External reporting, dataset uploads and training infrastructure are contextual dependencies; software names alone do not establish onboard execution. Ranked inference gives the top plausible configurations and supporting clues. Confidence is qualitative; vendor compatibility alone provides weak evidence of the actual installation. Confirmation steps appear in project dossiers.

comparison.title: An interrupted episode can lose its evidence
comparison.common: Mobile ALOHA holds an episode in RAM before HDF5; ToddlerBot saves in finally; OpenTeach depth/state arrays write after interruption. DROID queues incremental HDF5 writes and drains them on close.
comparison.difference: Persistence behavior varies within the same research workflow. File format alone does not describe what survives process failure.
comparison.implication: Record completion, buffered bytes, last persisted sample and termination reason. Test interruption and disk-full behavior per writer.

comparison.title: Hardware configuration belongs in the run record
comparison.common: The sample spans Orin hosts, Intel control PCs, remote inference servers and MCU sensor bridges. FAST-LIVO2 specifies a 32GB NUC; AnywhereVLA splits work across Orin and NUC; VibeCheck has separate sensor MCUs and a ROS2 host.
comparison.difference: A useful comparison identifies which process ran on which machine and the settings actually active during the run.
comparison.implication: Snapshot device, kernel, driver, memory, power mode, affinity and process placement at session start; report changes.

comparison.title: Readiness already has domain-specific meaning
comparison.common: MRS checks odometry, hardware freshness, arming and offboard mode; Mobile ALOHA waits for both grippers; Walk These Ways uses operator calibration gates.
comparison.difference: Starting processes is only one stage. Preserve existing readiness checks and their results as part of the attempt.
comparison.implication: Adapters for setup → ready → active → stop → finalize, with timestamps, ownership and failure reasons.

comparison.title: Capture formats are plural—even within one run
comparison.common: OpenTeach combines AVI, HDF5 and metadata; UMI combines a replay buffer, MP4 and a Zarr dataset; BeyondMimic configures MCAP. ACFR adds file splitting and compression controls.
comparison.difference: Adoption requires linking existing artifacts. A common session identity can span their different formats and storage paths.
comparison.implication: An artifact index with schemas, time ranges, checksums, source process and finalization state; adapters for existing recorders.

comparison.title: Existing resource controls are an integration surface
comparison.common: TidyBot sets real-time kernel/governor policy; Cheetah configures scheduler/memory locking; iiwa_setup pins logical CPUs; Upkie uses real-time scheduling.
comparison.difference: The survey supports observing and checking effective policy. It does not measure how often contention causes failed experiments.
comparison.implication: Explain requested versus effective settings, then attach latency and sensor-age evidence to the run.

comparison.title: Replay has several meanings
comparison.common: DROID has physical action playback with calibration warnings; MUSE documents rosbag clock replay; UMI stores training episodes; AutoEval stores per-episode trajectories and metadata.
comparison.difference: An artifact’s existence leaves questions about restartability, physical reset state and comparison validity.
comparison.implication: Declare replay mode and prerequisites; compare model/configuration, calibration, initial state, intervention and excluded-attempt history.

projects.provenance: Joint order/impedance parameters embedded in ONNX metadata; local policy path or W&B run selects model; generated controller config resolves policy path.

projects.resources: 50 Hz policy / 20 ms budget, 200 Hz CAN loop; 20 Hz operator / 50 ms budget. Rig reserves disjoint CPU sets: real_env 5, cameras 3, monitor 9, grippers 1, recorder 2. Video refuses start below 1 GB disk free; below 0.5 GB closes files early.
projects.ipc: NNG telemetry :9870, navigation :9873, arm/gaze :9874; JPEG cameras :5555/:5556; msgpack plan/MPC :9880; Unix IPC gripper request/status and detection sockets.

projects.readiness: CAN buses ERROR-ACTIVE; remote probe requires three PASS cases. Plan server warmup ~40 s until listening; first solve adds ~3.5 s CUDA graph capture.
projects.recovery: Nav silence stops base; arm silence returns home; gaze silence parks cameras. Frozen arm feedback latches damped hold. Remote CUDA fault has explicit stop/start and re-probe workflow.
projects.recording: Telemetry pickle on shutdown contains copied states/actions/IMU/targets/temperatures and optional Vicon. Camera recorder writes two 1280×720 MP4v files at 30 fps: starts on first gaze packet; stops after moved camera returns within 0.08 rad for 3 s, or arm/gaze stream silence for 3 s; automatically re-arms.
projects.buffering: Per-tick arrays copied into unbounded in-memory list; pickle written on save/shutdown, with no periodic flush in writer. CPU tensor copy prevents stored rows aliasing live sensor buffers.
projects.provenance: Pickle embeds full config/config_path, torque_limit, kp/kd, action_scale, joint_names, control_freq and gravity compensation; timestamp/task filename. Release supplies source pins and bundle MANIFEST.md5; captured session build/calibration hashes unresolved.
projects.limitations: Lab hardware table identifies X1-470; vendor mapping supplies CPU model. Installed RAM and remote planning GPU remain unpublished. Remote planner imports unpublished modules; crash flush and feedback freshness remain unresolved.

projects.software: openpilot release image installed to a supported comma device and supported car/harness. Onroad process manager gates most driving processes on started/on-road state; uploader runs continuously. The branch/release URL is configurable during setup.
projects.resources: The manager supervises a fixed process set; loggerd, deleter and uploader are separate managed processes. No per-process cgroup quota appears in these source files. Local logs live under the device log root, with disk cleanup controlled by free-space thresholds.
projects.ipc: openpilot daemons communicate through cereal/Cap’n Proto services over its messaging layer; loggerd subscribes to the configured service sockets and writes the selected messages. Manager polls deviceState, carParams and pandaStates, then publishes managerState.
projects.timing: Logger routes start/stop with ignition. loggerd rotates segments with the camera encoders at 60-second length; when encoder alignment stalls it can rotate after 1.2 segment lengths or when camera packets have been absent beyond its patience timeout.
projects.lifecycle: At manager start, stored transition parameters are cleared and build/device identity is recorded. The manager polls deviceState each second, starts/stops configured processes on off-road/on-road transitions, and publishes process status. loggerd is eligible on-road for a vehicle; uploader and deleter run off-road too.
projects.recovery: The process API stops a child with SIGINT, waits five seconds, then escalates to SIGKILL. ManagerState publishes running, shouldBeRunning and exit code. In the inspected manager reconciliation path, an exited child remains represented by its process object until a stop transition clears it; the code path does not immediately respawn it on unexpected exit. The uploader retries failed network transfers with exponential backoff capped at 120 seconds.
projects.readiness: DeviceState.started is the manager gate for on-road processes; CarParams distinguishes a car from non-car mode for logging. Supported-device/car/harness requirements are in setup documentation, and manager publishes live process state for UI/monitoring.
projects.placement: Perception and driving control run in openpilot processes on the comma device. loggerd writes on-device route segments; uploader transfers selected files after local completion. Developer PCs are used for analysis and replay.
projects.recording: loggerd subscribes to selected cereal services and writes rlog messages plus decimated qlog records. Camera encoders write H.265 road, wide-road and cabin videos. Segments rotate at 60 seconds; encoder alignment waits for participating streams and timeout fallback avoids indefinitely long segments.
projects.recordingFormat: rlog.zst and qlog.zst, HEVC camera files, plus qcamera.ts; route identity combines device dongle ID and timestamp and segment number.
projects.buffering: Encoder messages are held in a per-stream queue up to 10 seconds at 20 FPS (200 packets), then overflow frames are dropped. Files remain local until upload; qlog/qcamera are prioritized, qlog and qcamera upload size limits are 25 MB and 5 MB. The deleter reclaims logs below 5 GB or 10% free, skips locked segments, and preserves bookmarked segments plus two predecessors.
projects.replay: Upstream tools can fetch route segments and replay their camera/log streams for debugging. Replay is an engineering workflow; sources do not claim deterministic reproduction across software/device versions.
projects.provenance: Manager writes openpilot version, Git commit/date, branch, remote, hardware serial and dongle ID to persistent parameters and binds corresponding values to cloud logs. Routes identify a dongle and timestamp; logger segment number and InitData are available during replay. The sources do not state signed build attestation or per-model hash capture.
projects.limitations: Qualcomm platform memory is an SoC maximum; installed device RAM capacity is not identified by the public device abstraction. Manager exposes process status but the inspected path does not restart a process after unexpected exit until its state is reset. Disk reclamation and uploader retry behavior are specified in code; fleet-wide retention policy remains server-side.
projects.opportunity: Join the existing route and build identifiers with device RAM/storage SKU, process exit state, disk-pressure events and upload acknowledgements to diagnose regressions by hardware/software cohort.
projects.buyer: AV fleet operations, vehicle platform engineering, and data infrastructure teams supporting instrumented customer or test vehicles.
projects.adoptionRisk: Capture and upload are integrated with safety-relevant on-road processes, local retention, and server eligibility rules. Any extension needs to preserve segment locks, bookmark preservation, privacy choices, and the existing disk-pressure behavior.

projects.name: EDGAR research vehicle: target-hardware autonomous driving experiments
projects.horizon: Research vehicle introduced 2023; TUM describes the platform and research as active, but hardware details are sourced to the public launch announcement.
projects.compute: TUM reports a central high-performance onboard computer with a 16-core AMD CPU, 132 GB RAM and NVIDIA RTX A6000. This configuration comes from TUM’s vehicle announcement.
projects.cpu: 16-core AMD CPU, according to TUM’s research-vehicle announcement; processor model and clock are not stated.
projects.gpu: One NVIDIA RTX A6000 is reported as the onboard GPU in TUM’s announcement.
projects.memory: 132 GB RAM reported for the vehicle’s central computer; memory type and allocation are unspecified.
projects.software: Autoware-based autonomous-driving stack on EDGAR, developed and tested through simulation and real-vehicle use. TUM identifies ROS 2 as the modular integration layer; its CommonRoad interface is a ROS 2 planning module used for EDGAR planning research.
projects.resources: TUM reports a single x86 onboard server processing the synchronized vehicle data; platform announcement specifies 16-core AMD CPU, 132 GB RAM, RTX A6000. Separate vehicle data center/simulator are used in development; the public account does not specify storage allocation or process quotas.
projects.ipc: TUM describes ROS 2-based modular software and a CommonRoad planning module integrated as an Autoware planning component. TUM reports PTP-synchronized data processed on a single x86 onboard server; per-process topic topology and network details are not specified.
projects.timing: TUM AV Evaluation identifies end-to-end latency and its software-performance effects as a research focus. The vehicle announcement reports computer resources; public sources do not provide numeric runtime deadline or latency budget.
projects.lifecycle: TUM describes a development loop from virtual tests and simulation to selected real-vehicle tests. The EDGAR digital-twin repo contains a launch description for Autoware and CARLA/HIL workflows; its Docker compose commands describe simulation/HIL setup, while public docs do not establish physical-car boot and update automation.
projects.recovery: Public sources reviewed do not specify process supervisor, watchdog, restart behavior, failover, or fault-recovery procedures for the installed vehicle computer.
projects.readiness: Research software is exercised in simulation and then applied under real conditions on a Level-5-capable research vehicle with longitudinal/lateral actuation interfaces. Detailed operator checklist and readiness gate are not public in the reviewed pages.
projects.placement: Autonomous-driving software runs on the central onboard HPC computer. Matching computer hardware is embedded in the simulation environment for development and automated pre-test validation.
projects.recording: The active vehicle data practice reported by the EDGAR team is route-wide ROS bag capture with camera excluded for GDPR and PTP synchronization. Separately, a Feb 2026 CommonRoad evaluation-pipeline brief asks the development team to implement a ROS 2 MCAP recorder using existing example code; the brief classifies this as project work.
projects.recordingFormat: Existing route capture: ROS bag, camera excluded in the shared dataset. Evaluation-pipeline work: ROS 2 MCAP recorder example and conversion to CommonRoad scenario; the brief scopes development of this workflow.
projects.buffering: TUM’s inspected vehicle and recording sources leave recorder buffering, storage capacity, and retention unspecified.
projects.replay: The evaluation project scopes reading a CommonRoad planning problem, automatically triggering EDGAR in simulation, recording simulated driving, and spawning scenario traffic. TUM’s CommonRoad interface is also a ROS 2 Autoware planning component used for EDGAR planning research.
projects.provenance: Route capture is PTP synchronized and stored as ROS bag; the evaluation task maps MCAP into CommonRoad scenarios and planning problems. Public sources do not define per-run vehicle software commit, calibration manifest, or a stable identifier linking every bag, scenario and simulator run.
projects.limitations: TUM publishes installed compute, sensor inventory, synchronized route-wide bag capture, ROS 2/Autoware integration, and a simulator loop. The 2026 MCAP/CommonRoad workflow appears in a development brief with example code; completed rollout status requires confirmation. Public sources leave storage quota, run naming, and physical vehicle boot/recovery steps open.
projects.opportunity: Join each route bag or MCAP-derived scenario with Autoware/CommonRoad commits, vehicle and calibration identity, PTP health, and simulator trigger/run ID so engineers can trace differences between road and simulation evaluations.
projects.buyer: TUM AV research groups and research-vehicle operations teams evaluating integrated autonomy on public roads.
projects.adoptionRisk: The MCAP recorder and scenario-trigger workflow are scoped as research development tasks; confirm implementation status and ROS bag compatibility with current vehicle data. Any added capture must preserve the camera privacy exclusion used for shared route datasets.

projects.name: AutoSDV physical reference vehicle: compact Autoware compute and safety lifecycle
projects.horizon: AutoSDV v0.1.0 stable release documents Autoware 2025.02, CUDA 12.3 and JetPack 6.0; public reference design is versioned and actively maintained.
projects.compute: AutoSDV documentation identifies this installed vehicle computer as a Jetson AGX Orin 64GB module with 1TB NVMe SSD. NVIDIA specifies the 64GB module configuration as 12-core Cortex-A78AE CPU, 2048 CUDA-core Ampere GPU and 64GB LPDDR5 at 204.8GB/s.
projects.cpu: Jetson AGX Orin 64GB module: 12-core 64-bit Arm Cortex-A78AE v8.2 CPU (3MB L2 + 6MB L3).
projects.gpu: Jetson AGX Orin 64GB module has 2048 NVIDIA Ampere CUDA cores and 64 Tensor Cores. AutoSDV’s release table separately pins CUDA 12.3 as an x86 build dependency.
projects.memory: Jetson AGX Orin 64GB module provides 64 GB 256-bit LPDDR5 with 204.8 GB/s bandwidth. NVIDIA lists 64 GB eMMC on the module; AutoSDV separately documents 1TB NVMe storage.
projects.software: Autoware.universe on ROS 2 Humble. AutoSDV v0.1.0 pins Autoware 2025.02, CUDA 12.3 (x86 compatibility entry), and JetPack 6.0 as version dependencies.
projects.resources: Physical platform documentation lists 1TB NVMe, while NVIDIA’s module spec lists 64GB eMMC. AutoSDV launcher and MRM configuration run with the onboard Autoware stack; process CPU/GPU quotas and recorder allocation are unspecified in those sources.
projects.ipc: ROS 2 topics provide the Autoware vehicle/sensor interfaces. Exact process/container IPC and DDS configuration for the physical platform are not established by the general reference page.
projects.timing: Platform documents a 40-minute battery life; sources reviewed do not state control loop deadline, sensor synchronization tolerance, or recording throughput.
projects.lifecycle: Versioned setup uses AutoSDV launcher and release-defined dependencies. Autoware system configuration includes diagnostics and MRM handlers/operators. Public guides document software setup and safety configuration, but not atomic OTA, rollback, or a complete power-on-to-drive supervisor.
projects.recovery: MRM configuration distinguishes emergency-stop and comfortable-stop operators, with availability/status exposed through Autoware operation-mode interfaces. A lab guide notes localization accuracy checking is disabled in its tested configuration due to false emergency stops; this applies to that tested deployment.
projects.readiness: Autoware MRM/status interfaces and diagnostics contribute to startup/operation readiness; guide demonstrates checking operation-mode availability. Exact pre-drive checklist and independent safety controller architecture are not established.
projects.placement: Autoware navigation and sensor processing target the onboard Jetson. Repository additionally describes x86 build compatibility; build host should remain distinct from installed vehicle computer.
projects.recording: Autoware’s official control-data collection workflow records relevant control, vehicle, and IMU topics to a ROS bag during supervised acceleration/braking, then validates recorded data. AutoSDV page itself does not claim this tool is preinstalled or run automatically on every drive.
projects.recordingFormat: ROS 2 bag. The official Autoware tool documents topics matching control, vehicle, and IMU regular expressions and names output using maneuver/target value plus wall-clock timestamp.
projects.buffering: No recorder queue depth, storage partition, retention, disk-full behavior, or upload policy is specified in the reviewed AutoSDV/Autoware docs; 1TB NVMe is platform capacity only.
projects.replay: Autoware tools use ROS bags for offline calibration/analysis; ROS 2 bag playback is a standard path, but exact AutoSDV drive-to-replay launch configuration was not confirmed from cited pages.
projects.provenance: AutoSDV release pins Autoware/CUDA/JetPack versions; collection filename encodes maneuver, target acceleration and timestamp. Per-run source commit, map/sensor calibration digest, device identity, and firmware hash binding are not established.
projects.limitations: AutoSDV is a 1/10-scale research and education vehicle. Its hardware configuration is explicit; the Autoware collection tool is a maneuver-oriented ROS bag workflow, while platform docs do not describe an always-on drive logger or disk-retention policy.
projects.opportunity: Practical target for repeatable experiment bundles that join ROS bags with pinned software versions, map/sensor calibration identity, readiness/MRM state, and storage health. The reference stack offers known onboard compute and a reproducible release baseline.
projects.buyer: Autonomy labs and education programs adopting AutoSDV or similar Autoware-powered low-speed platforms; platform integrators maintaining Jetson-based test vehicles.
projects.adoptionRisk: Open reference platform and ROS 2 bag tooling make integration feasible, but logging tool behavior is maneuver-specific and safety/MRM configurations can be locally modified. Verify exact release, hardware, localization diagnostics, and recorder workload on the physical car.

projects.name: VOXL 2 integrated PX4 and ROS 2 companion flight workflow
projects.compute: VOXL 2 combines a QRB5165 application processor running Linux with PX4 on the sensors DSP (SLPI); a separate flight controller is optional. This split keeps flight-control firmware and Linux autonomy on distinct processors.
projects.cpu: QRB5165, 8 cores up to 3.091 GHz (application processor).
projects.gpu: Adreno 650 GPU, 1024 ALU; 15 TOPS NPU listed separately by ModalAI.
projects.memory: 8 GB LPDDR5 and 128 GB flash on VOXL 2; product matrix specifies Ubuntu 18.04 and Linux kernel 4.19.
projects.software: VOXL SDK services, PX4 on SLPI and ROS 2 Foxy packages; voxl-mpa-to-ros2 converts camera, IMU, point-cloud and VIO data. The vendor documents SDK/PX4 version-dependent MicroDDS client names, so firmware and message packages must be paired.
projects.resources: The board provides QRB5165 compute, cameras, flash, and a shared onboard service environment. `voxl-inspect-services` reports service enable/running state and a CPU-use snapshot; ModalAI cautions that this is momentary and recommends `top` for process-level utilization. Service resource reservations are unspecified in the MPA guide.
projects.ipc: Linux services exchange MPA data through POSIX named pipes under `/run/mpa/`; libmodal_pipe supports dedicated client pipes, control/request pipes, and pipe-info JSON. Large images can use shared ION/DMA buffers to avoid copies. PX4-to-ROS 2 separately uses a localhost UDP uXRCE-DDS agent/client on port 8888.
projects.timing: libmodal_pipe exposes RT-priority thread creation, CPU-affinity helpers, and `mpa_nanosleep`/`mpa_loop_sleep`; `modal-pipe-ping` is a supplied latency-measurement example. VOXL docs reviewed do not publish a measured application-to-actuator latency for the figure-eight example.
projects.lifecycle: MPA services are systemd services enabled according to SKU configuration. PX4 starts its uXRCE-DDS client at boot in the documented SDK 1.8 setup. For flight logs, `voxl-logger.service` can record only while armed; alternatively `voxl-logger-auto` runs persistently, accepts start/stop/status/arm-trigger commands, creates one `logNNNN/` directory per trigger, and supports an auto-stop duration. Service changes can be inspected with `voxl-inspect-services` and investigated through the journal.
projects.recovery: ModalAI documents an operator recovery loop: inspect enabled/running services, read the systemd journal, check whether the upstream `/run/mpa/` pipe exists, and start/restart a service or run its binary in the foreground. The docs do not specify a common automatic restart/backoff contract for every service.
projects.readiness: The VIO flight checklist requires camera server, selected VIO server, vision hub and portal services; verify tracking-camera detection, inspect VIO feature/trajectory output, perform a hand-held low-drift test, compare post-extrinsics pose to PX4 local position, and check MAVLink odometry at PX4. The source recommends repeating the hand-held test after a VIO switch before flight.
projects.placement: PX4 runs on the onboard sensors DSP; Linux ROS 2 autonomy and vision services run on the same VOXL 2 board. A ground computer can connect over an add-on network interface; network hardware is not built in.
projects.recording: There are separate application and flight records. `voxl-logger` stores MPA samples under `/data/voxl-logger/` by default; camera images are lossless PNG for grayscale and JPG for color, with optional raw channels in `data.raw`. Triggered mode writes `logNNNN/` sessions with a note in `info.json`, plus configurable named pipes. PX4 ULog files are under `/data/px4/log`; the VOXL 2 defaults set `SDLOG_PROFILE=2083` (default, estimator replay, debug, and high-rate sensor sets). A host-side `voxl-logger-to-rosbag` package converts MPA logs into ROS topics.
projects.buffering: Logger auto config can skip N of every N+1 samples and enforce `max_duration_s`; it checks free disk space before and during capture and stops when space runs low. PX4 topic profiles select capture sets/rates. MPA pipe types define recommended read-buffer and pipe sizes; image consumers can share ION buffers, released after the callback by default or manually when retained. The docs do not claim a lossless capture guarantee under overload.
projects.replay: `voxl-replay -p <log_dir>` republishes logged MPA pipes and can select/exclude pipes, start/finish times, or a camera frame offset; it can publish camera data as ION buffers. Open-VINS tools can replay a capture through the in-process estimator and write per-frame CSV and a summary; `voxl-benchmark-vio` automates per-log estimator runs and merges pose/CPU metrics. PX4 `.ulg` remains a separate flight-control record.
projects.provenance: A session gets a numbered `logNNNN` directory and optional note in `info.json`; PX4 parameters are persisted under `/data/px4/param/parameters`, and PX4 ULog records include system/software/board and parameter metadata. ModalAI documents `voxl-inspect-services -v` for package versions and `-j` for machine-readable service state. The docs do not require combining those records into a single immutable flight manifest.
projects.limitations: The MPA and recorder provide a concrete onboard capture/replay loop, storage guard, and service inspection. Public docs still leave application-level synchronization across MPA logs, PX4 ULog and ROS bags to the operator; they do not state capture-drop guarantees or a unified run manifest.
projects.horizon: Current vendor platform documentation, checked October 2026; SDK and PX4 compatibility are version-sensitive.
projects.opportunity: A unified run record could link PX4 ULog, ROS 2 camera/VIO streams, calibration, software versions, and flight session identity for repeatable onboard perception trials.
projects.buyer: UAS autonomy teams, defense and public-safety integrators, and research groups standardizing onboard AI compute.
projects.adoptionRisk: The integrated split-processor stack is vendor-specific; SDK image, PX4 branch, ROS distribution, and versioned message compatibility can constrain upgrades and portability.

projects.name: Auterion Skynode S PX4 mission-computer deployment and flight-log workflow
projects.compute: Skynode S packages a Linux mission computer and PX4 flight stack into one 14 g PCBA (24 g with heatsink). PX4 can send its flight log over MAVLink to the companion computer; Skynode S has no SD card, so onboard log storage is companion-side only.
projects.cpu: Quad-core ARM Cortex-A53 at 1.8 GHz.
projects.gpu: No general-purpose GPU is listed in the Skynode S datasheet; it does specify hardware H.264/H.265 encoding for two 1080p60 streams and an NPU rated at 2.3 TOPS.
projects.memory: 4 GB LPDDR4 and 32 GB eMMC. Auterion states 4–6 W for the loaded CPU device without peripherals; total input power is capped at 30 W with peripherals.
projects.software: Auterion Enterprise (AOS) plus PX4. Auterion documents production and development images, with production image access restrictions for shell, debug UART and PX4 parameter changes.
projects.resources: The module provides shared 5 V peripheral power, with a 25 W maximum across peripherals. CPU affinity, per-process memory budgets and onboard recorder resource use are not published in the reviewed documentation.
projects.ipc: PX4 SDLOG_BACKEND can stream ULog over MAVLink to the companion computer. Auterion Mission Control can receive that stream at the ground station; the cited docs do not specify ROS 2 transport or a message bridge for mission applications.
projects.timing: The vendor describes log streaming as continuously updated from arm through disarm, but publishes no stream latency, sample-rate guarantee, storage throughput, or ROS/control timing measurements in the cited material.
projects.lifecycle: PX4 logs by arming session. Operators can enable automatic MAVLink 2.0 logging in Mission Control; the current .ulg appears in its local logs folder and updates until disarm. Auterion ships production and development image variants.
projects.recovery: PX4 exposes configurable low-battery, datalink-loss, RC-loss and geofence actions. The reviewed materials do not describe supervision or restart behavior for the companion logger, and the live stream is not automatically uploaded to Auterion Suite.
projects.readiness: The docs specify production-image protections and PX4 failsafe parameters, but no single Skynode preflight readiness report or cross-service health check for mission computer, recorder, GNSS, and application is documented.
projects.placement: PX4 flight control and the AOS mission computer are integrated on Skynode S; PX4 flight logs stream over MAVLink to Auterion Mission Control on the ground-control station. The ground-station copy is not automatically mirrored to Auterion Suite in the described flow.
projects.recording: PX4 flight logs use ULog (.ulg). Mission Control saves a live, continuously updated .ulg on the ground station from arming until disarming; for Skynode S, SD-card logging is unavailable, so log data is stored on the companion side.
projects.buffering: PX4 supports topic-rate selection and logging profiles; Auterion's Skynode S documentation does not state the companion log buffer size, write queue depth, overflow counter, or recovery after a broken link.
projects.replay: ULog supports post-flight inspection. The Auterion guide documents log listing and streaming; reconstruction of mission application inputs is unspecified.
projects.provenance: ULog contains PX4 system, hardware, software and parameter metadata. Auterion documents the option to omit position/GPS fields; the docs caution that doing so removes information useful for incident analysis. No application/container digest or mission manifest is mandated by this workflow.
projects.limitations: The hardware and logging path are documented, but the cited sources do not quantify mission workload performance, logger buffering, onboard ROS integration, or automated recovery from companion/ground-link failure. On Skynode S, logging depends on the companion-side path because there is no FMU SD-card logging.
projects.horizon: Current Auterion documentation, checked October 2026; image and PX4 parameter behavior should be tied to the deployed release.
projects.opportunity: A flight package could join the streamed ULog with AOS image identity, mission configuration, application build, and recorder-link health to support incident review and fleet comparison.
projects.buyer: Commercial UAS manufacturers, regulated enterprise operators, and integrators building secure aircraft around Auterion's avionics stack.
projects.adoptionRisk: The lack of a Skynode S SD-card path makes log availability depend on companion storage and, for ground copies, MAVLink connectivity; production-image controls and privacy settings also shape data access.

projects.name: TU Delft Event-Orin event-camera drone and MCAP flight-capture workflow
projects.compute: An 822 g quadrotor couples a Jetson Orin NX 16 GB companion (62 g; measured around 9 W by the project with `jtop`) to a Holybro Kakute H7 Mini running PX4. It carries an iniVation DVXplorer Micro event camera and Intel RealSense D435i stereo camera; a MicoAir MTF-01 supplies optical flow/range.
projects.cpu: Jetson Orin NX 16 GB: NVIDIA specifies eight Arm Cortex-A78AE CPU cores, configured at up to 2 GHz in the cited module-emulation technical note.
projects.gpu: Jetson Orin NX 16 GB: 1024-core NVIDIA Ampere GPU with 32 Tensor Cores; the project installs JetPack 6.0 and builds CUDA/PyTorch containers.
projects.memory: Jetson Orin NX module has 16 GB LPDDR5 shared memory. The project also names a Corsair MP600 Core Mini SSD for onboard storage; capacity is not given in the README.
projects.software: Ubuntu 22.04 on JetPack 6.0 / Jetson Linux 36.3, ROS 2 Humble, PX4 firmware built for `holybro_kakuteh7mini_default`, MAVLink Router, micro XRCE-DDS Agent, and a Jetson container with CUDA 12.2/PyTorch 2.4 example dependencies. The project uses event-camera `libcaer_driver` and RealSense ROS packages.
projects.resources: The flight log reports 9 W approximate Jetson draw from `jtop`; the board uses MAXN mode and max fan at boot. The complete 822 g airframe has a listed 213.2 W approximate total, mostly propulsion. No process-level CPU, GPU, RAM, or storage quota is stated.
projects.ipc: PX4 telemetry/ground-station path uses MAVLink Router over FC TELEM1 to TCP port 5760; the repo says 921600 baud worked where higher baud caused offboard control issues. PX4-to-ROS 2 uses micro XRCE-DDS Agent over TELEM2 `/dev/ttyTHS3` at 3,000,000 baud. ROS event-camera driver and recorder are composed in one ROS 2 component container with intra-process communication enabled.
projects.timing: The event camera driver publishes event messages at a 1 ms message-time threshold and sets message-size threshold to zero for immediate publish. Its statistics interval is 2 s. UARTs use 921600 and 3,000,000 baud respectively. These settings are documented; no sensor-to-setpoint end-to-end latency or flight-control deadline is measured.
projects.lifecycle: `drone_flight.sh` creates a tmux session with MAVLink Router, serial XRCE-DDS Agent, an interactive project container, and `htop`. The operator starts the ROS 2 flight recorder launch, checks QGroundControl modes, flies in Position or Stabilized mode, lands, stops rosbag and closes windows. `move_logs_to_drive.sh` copies recorded bags and MAVLink logs to the configured USB UUID, then unmounts it.
projects.recovery: The runbook relies on tmux terminals and operator inspection; it provides no service supervisor or automatic restart for the container, agent, router, or recorder. RC and QGroundControl remain part of the flight setup. The log-export script checks mount/copy errors and exits on failed mount or copy, but deletes each source after successful copy.
projects.readiness: The operator checks ROS/container build, QGroundControl TCP link, flight-mode configuration, sensor/device detection, and PX4 custom-mode registration with `commander status`. The project notes camera rate limits and warns that 921600 baud was needed on TELEM1 where higher rates caused offboard issues. There is no single automated preflight result or data-recorder health gate.
projects.placement: Onboard Orin runs ROS 2, sensor drivers, recorder, MAVLink Router and XRCE-DDS Agent; the Kakute H7 Mini runs PX4. The ground station runs QGroundControl (tested under Windows 11/WSL Ubuntu 22.04). Bags and MAVLink logs are staged on the Orin and manually transferred to USB after landing.
projects.recording: `drone_flight_recorder.launch.py` records MCAP via rosbag2 from event-camera `/event_camera/events` and `/event_camera/imu`, plus PX4 actuator motors, hover thrust estimate, vehicle odometry, attitude, and angular velocity topics. The recorder starts immediately with prefix `ros/rosbags/rosbag2_`. Flight steps explicitly stop bag recording before closing windows; PX4/MAVLink logs are also copied from `~/mavlink_logs/`.
projects.buffering: The composable rosbag2 recorder is configured with `max_cache_size=100*1024*1024` bytes and `storage_id=mcap`. The event camera publishes with a 1 ms message-time threshold, immediate publication by size threshold 0, and a default spatial subsample step of 3 (described as 4x). Recorder drop policy, saturation counters and disk-space preflight are not configured in this launch file.
projects.replay: The project says to inspect recorded bags in Foxglove or convert them to HDF5. It provides PX4/Gazebo simulation scripts for testing modes, but the reviewed physical-flight instructions do not provide a deterministic physical-input replay recipe or bind replay to a flight manifest.
projects.provenance: The repository pins PX4 submodule `795c22f`, `px4_msgs` `58e372c`, the PX4 ROS 2 interface library `7b0162d`, and composable recorder `b398a6b`. The log filename uses a `rosbag2_` prefix; the launch leaves `bag_name` empty and supplies no flight ID, run metadata sidecar, or camera calibration/config hash in the recorder settings.
projects.limitations: This is an operator-run research platform with explicit avionics links, a composed MCAP event/flight-state recorder, cache size, and USB export script. The guide has no automatic service recovery, recorder saturation/drop accounting, unified session manifest, or deterministic flight replay procedure; its export script deletes onboard source records after successful copy.
projects.horizon: Current public repository inspected October 2026; the README records JetPack 6.0 / Jetson Linux 36.3 and the linked submodule revisions, so deployments should preserve their exact checkout and board image.
projects.opportunity: An experiment service could turn its manual tmux/ROS launch workflow into a session contract that checks recorder and sensor health, stamps the MCAP with the pinned PX4/ROS/container and calibration identity, and verifies exported copies before pruning onboard logs.
projects.buyer: University aerial robotics labs and event-camera/visual-inertial research groups that need synchronized onboard sensor and flight-controller data.
projects.adoptionRisk: The stack is a custom, operator-maintained platform with hand-configured serial devices, containers and USB offload; high sensor volume and small-drone power/thermal limits make recorder health and verified log transfer operationally important.

These artifacts describe the published OpenPI DROID evaluation script and optional policy recorder. They expose per-rollout and per-inference capture paths.

runtime.value: Separate Python environments for the GPU policy server and DROID robot client; camera IDs configured in main.py.
Separate Python environments for the GPU policy server and DROID robot client; camera IDs configured in main.py.
DROID loop sleeps to target 15 Hz; client resizes inference images to 224×224. The example contains no CPU affinity or cgroup configuration.
Synchronous WebSocket request/reply with MessagePack/NumPy serialization; compression disabled. Server returns a chunk of actions per observation.
Default executes 8 actions before the next policy request; target 15 Hz. Server replies include infer_ms and previous request total time.

lifecycle.value: Start serve_policy.py on the GPU host, then scripts/main.py on the control laptop. Host/port and checkpoint are CLI arguments; default port 8000.
Client retries connection-refused every 5 s during startup. DROID defers Ctrl+C until inference returns, ends rollout, and then saves video.
Server exposes /healthz and sends model metadata on connection. Operator chooses cameras, enters an instruction, then starts the rollout.
RobotEnv controls the Franka from the DROID environment; GPU inference runs in a separate network process. openpi-client carries observations/actions.
These artifacts describe the published OpenPI DROID evaluation script and optional policy recorder. They expose per-rollout and per-inference capture paths.

recording.value: DROID example: H.264 MP4 per rollout, robot_camera_views.png, and results/eval_<timestamp>.csv. Server --record adds policy_records/step_<n>.npy.
Video frames accumulate in a Python list for the rollout (600-step default), then are stacked and encoded at 10 fps. CSV rows remain in memory until evaluation exits.
Ctrl+C ends the rollout before video encoding; CSV writes after the interactive evaluation loop. PolicyRecorder writes each inference synchronously with numpy.save.
Timestamped video/CSV paths; CSV stores success, duration (step index), video filename. Policy dump stores flattened inputs/outputs; step counter restarts at process startup.

lifecycle.value: The Jetson switcher manages labeled Docker applications, exposes list/status/switch/stop/update and Python ensure_running, and restores the prior application through systemd and state.json. It deliberately manages only its own containers. Its documented operating assumption is that the managed application runs alone: other containers must not monopolize GPU memory, utilization, or bandwidth. This is a useful design boundary, not evidence of observed customer failures. Related Stretch AI code uses latest-observation ZeroMQ delivery, and an episode recorder that buffers images before writing and records git/config/session metadata. Recording throughput and provenance on Stretch 4 still need confirmation.
